items.q: Facial weakness sparing the forehead most likely localises where?
items.exp: Forehead muscles receive bilateral cortical supply so central lesions spare forehead wrinkling, while peripheral nerve lesions weaken the entire face including forehead. Sparing demands stroke pathway assessment.
r: Incorrect. Mastoid nerve lesion weakens forehead too.
Correct. Forehead sparing means upper motor neuron lesion.
Incorrect. Parotid lesions are peripheral pattern.
Incorrect. Foramen exit lesion is lower motor neuron.
items.kp: Spare the forehead, suspect the brain.

items.q: Bell palsy treatment with best early evidence within 72 hours is what?
items.exp: Early prednisolone significantly raises complete recovery in Bell palsy; lubricants and night taping protect the cornea when blink fails. Antivirals alone lack benefit; surgery is exceptional.
r: Incorrect. No bacterial cause to treat.
Correct. Early steroids and eye care.
Incorrect. Decompression is rare selected case.
Incorrect. Eye damage is preventable and steroids help.

items.q: House Brackmann grade VI means what?
items.exp: Grade I is normal and grade VI is total paralysis with no tone or movement; intermediate grades track partial recovery used in prognosis and studies.
r: Incorrect. Normal is grade I.
Correct. VI equals total paralysis.
Incorrect. Mild weakness is grade II.
Incorrect. Synkinesis features in middle grades.
items.kp: One is normal, six is total.

items.q: Transverse temporal bone fracture typically causes which ear pattern?
o: Sensorineural loss with vertigo and facial palsy
items.exp: Transverse fractures cross otic capsule and meatus injuring cochlea, vestibule and facial nerve together. Longitudinal fractures instead follow canal causing conductive loss and CSF otorrhoea.
r: Incorrect. That is longitudinal or simple trauma pattern.
Correct. Transverse: sensorineural plus nerve injury.
Incorrect. Effusion is not fracture signature.
Incorrect. Otosclerosis is non traumatic fixation.
items.kp: Across the capsule: deaf, dizzy, weak face.

items.q: Crocodile tears after facial palsy recovery result from what?
o: Aberrant regeneration of salivary fibres to lacrimal gland
items.exp: Regrowing parasympathetic fibres meant for salivary glands misroute to lacrimal gland, so eating triggers tearing (gustatory lacrimation), a late aberrant regeneration sign like synkinesis.
r: Incorrect. Tumour causes mass not meal linked tears.
Correct. Miswired regeneration causes crocodile tears.
Incorrect. Blockage causes constant watering, not gustatory.
Incorrect. Allergy itches bilaterally.
items.kp: Tears at meals mean fibres rewired wrongly.

items.q: Facial palsy with discharging cholesteatoma ear should be managed how?
o: Urgent ENT care for surgical source control
items.exp: Otogenic palsy means infection or cholesteatoma compresses or invades the nerve in its canal; urgent mastoid surgery assessment plus antibiotics protects nerve and brain. Bell is diagnosis of exclusion.
r: Incorrect. Ear disease excludes simple Bell label.
Correct. Urgent surgical source control assessment.
Incorrect. Steroids without source control risk spread.
Incorrect. Massage does not remove cholesteatoma.
items.kp: Palsy plus cholesteatoma: operate the source urgently.

items.q: Most Bell palsy patients have which long term outcome?
items.exp: About 70 percent recover completely spontaneously and steroids raise that further; incomplete recovery leaves synkinesis or weakness in minority, worse with Ramsay Hunt and diabetes.
r: Incorrect. Total permanent loss is minority outcome.
Correct. Majority recover well.
Incorrect. Bilateral palsy suggests other causes.
Incorrect. Surgery is exceptional.
items.kp: Most Bell faces recover; Ramsay Hunt less so.

items.q: Inability to close the eye in facial palsy most urgently risks what?
items.exp: Failed blink and Bell phenomenon insufficiency dry and abrade cornea toward ulcer and perforation, so lubrication, taping, moisture chambers and ophthalmology referral are urgent. Others are branch symptoms.
r: Incorrect. Taste loss is chorda tympani symptom.
Correct. Corneal exposure is the urgent danger.
Incorrect. Hyperacusis is stapedius branch sign, not emergency.
Incorrect. Dry mouth follows gland fibre loss.
items.kp: Open eye in palsy: protect cornea first.

items.q: Hyperacusis in facial palsy localises lesion proximal to which branch?
items.exp: Stapedius normally dampens loud sound; lesion at or above its branch removes the reflex causing hyperacusis, helping segment localisation along with taste and tearing tests historically.
r: Incorrect. Chorda lesion loses taste and salivation.
Correct. Stapedius branch level gives hyperacusis.
Incorrect. Greater petrosal affects tearing earlier.
Incorrect. Parotid branches are distal motor only.
items.kp: Loud hurts when stapedius branch is out.

items.q: Slowly progressive facial palsy over months should prompt search for what?
items.exp: Bell palsy peaks within days; progression beyond three weeks, recurrence, spasm or mass suggests neoplasm (parotid malignancy, schwannoma) needing imaging and referral, not idiopathic label.
r: Incorrect. Bell peaks in days, not months.
Correct. Slow progression means tumour until excluded.
Incorrect. Colds do not slowly paralyse.
Incorrect. Wax never weakens facial nerve.
items.kp: Slow weak face equals tumour hunt.
